--- title: "Week 10 Exercises" distributed: 2026-10-27 show-hints: true --- ## Simulate and Recover; Ordered Logit {ref="sim-recover-ordered"} One important way to test and develop your understanding of statistical models and quantities of interest is to *simulate* a fake data set with known true quantity of interest (e.g., coefficients or first difference) and then *recover* that quantity of interest through your estimation procedure. In Week 9, we did this for logit. See [Simulate and Recover; Logit](wk09-exercises.html#ex-8). Do this for the ordered logit model in the [notes](https://pos5747.github.io/notes/wk06/03-ordered-logit.html). As your quantity of interest, use $\Pr(y \geq 3)$ when `income` equals 1.5 and `x2` equals `"Label 1"`. 1. First, simulate a fake data set with known cutpoints, coefficients, and quantity of interest. Write this code yourself; adapt your Week 9 code. Notice that the linear predictor `eta` has no intercept. The cutpoints `alpha` take its place. In the solution, I use the values below, but you can choose different values if you like (keep 1.5 among the values of `income`). - `n` = 10,000. - `income`: −2.5, −1.5, −0.5, 0.5, 1.5, or 2.5, equally likely. - `x2`: `"Label 1"` (about 75%) or `"Label 2"` (about 25%). - Cutpoints `alpha`: −1, 0.5, and 2 (so four categories). - Coefficients: 0.4 for `income`; 1 for `x2` = `"Label 2"`. - `y` an ordered factor, in a data frame named `data`. - Compute the true $\Pr(y \geq 3)$ from the true values. 1. Second, use `MASS::polr()` to fit an ordered logit model to the fake data. Are the true cutpoints and coefficients inside their 95% confidence intervals? (`polr()` calls the cutpoints "Intercepts" and labels them `1|2`, `2|3`, and `3|4`.) 1. Third, use `predictions()` to recover the true quantity of interest. Is the true value inside the 95% CI? 1. Fourth, adapt the code to compute the true first difference in $\Pr(y \geq 3)$ as `income` moves from −1.5 to 1.5 (with `x2` equal to `"Label 1"`). Then recover it with `comparisons()`. 1. Fifth, refit the model with `brm(family = cumulative("logit"))`. Recover the cutpoints, the coefficients, and the first difference. Compare with `polr()` and the truth. ::: hint $\Pr(y \geq 3)$ is the sum of the probabilities of categories 3 and 4. - Week 6 added up category probabilities with `hypothesis`: [Red State, Blue State: Part 2(a)](wk06-exercises.html#ex-8), part 3. ::: ::: sol **Part 1** Your code will differ. Here is one version. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # --- simulate a fake data set --- # set seed for reproducibility set.seed(1234) # set sample size n <- 10000 # needs to be large enough so that CI isn't super wide # create explanatory variables ## numeric variable; six brackets, like income in the anes data income <- sample(c(-2.5, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5), size = n, replace = TRUE) ## qualitative variable x2 <- sample(c("Label 1", "Label 2"), size = n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.75, 0.25)) # about 75% will be "Label 1" # create cutpoints and coefficients alpha <- c(-1, 0.5, 2) # J - 1 = 3 cutpoints, so J = 4 categories b1 <- 0.4 b2 <- 1 # linear predictor; no intercept! eta <- b1*income + b2*(x2 == "Label 2") # cumulative probabilities Pr(y <= j), j = 1, 2, 3 cp1 <- plogis(alpha[1] - eta) cp2 <- plogis(alpha[2] - eta) cp3 <- plogis(alpha[3] - eta) # category probabilities Pr(y = j), j = 1, 2, 3, 4; one row per observation p <- cbind(cp1, cp2 - cp1, cp3 - cp2, 1 - cp3) # simulate outcome for ordered logit model; one draw per observation y <- numeric(n) for (i in 1:n) { y[i] <- sample(1:4, size = 1, prob = p[i, ]) } # combine into data frame; y must be an ordered factor for polr() data <- data.frame(y = factor(y, ordered = TRUE), income, x2) # truth: Pr(y >= 3) when income = 1.5 and x2 = "Label 1" eta_c <- b1*1.5 # x2 = "Label 1", so the b2 term is zero 1 - plogis(alpha[2] - eta_c) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5249792 ``` ::: ::: The true value of $\Pr(y \geq 3)$ is about 0.525. Notice that $\Pr(y \geq 3) = 1 - \Pr(y \leq 2) = 1 - \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_2 - \eta)$, so we only need the second cutpoint. **Part 2** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # fit ordered logit model fit <- MASS::polr(y ~ income + x2, data = data, Hess = TRUE) # estimates and 95% cis for the coefficients and the cutpoints est <- c(coef(fit), fit$zeta) se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit))) cbind(truth = c(b1, b2, alpha), estimate = est, lower = est - 1.96*se, upper = est + 1.96*se) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` truth estimate lower upper income 0.4 0.409 0.387 0.431 x2Label 2 1.0 0.923 0.839 1.006 1|2 -1.0 -1.000 -1.051 -0.950 2|3 0.5 0.511 0.464 0.558 3|4 2.0 2.018 1.956 2.080 ``` ::: ::: All five true values are inside their 95% confidence intervals. The true value of `b2` (i.e., 1) is only barely inside its interval (about 0.84 to 1.01); across many simulated data sets, we'd expect the interval to miss the true value about 5% of the time. **Part 3** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # recover Pr(y >= 3) when income = 1.5 and x2 = "Label 1" predictions(fit, newdata = datagrid(income = 1.5, x2 = "Label 1"), hypothesis = "b3 + b4 = 0") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % b3+b4=0 0.526 0.00709 74.2 <0.001 Inf 0.512 0.54 Type: probs ``` ::: ::: The estimate is about 0.526, and the 95% CI runs from about 0.512 to 0.540. The true value (about 0.525) is inside the interval, as it usually will be. **Part 4** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # truth: fd in Pr(y >= 3) as income moves from -1.5 to 1.5; x2 = "Label 1" pr_hi <- 1 - plogis(alpha[2] - b1*1.5) pr_lo <- 1 - plogis(alpha[2] - b1*(-1.5)) pr_hi - pr_lo ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.2752393 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # recover this fd comparisons(fit, variables = list(income = c(-1.5, 1.5)), newdata = datagrid(x2 = "Label 1"), hypothesis = "b3 + b4 = 0") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % b3+b4=0 0.28 0.00746 37.6 <0.001 1025.9 0.266 0.295 Type: probs ``` ::: ::: The true first difference is about 0.275. The estimate is about 0.280, and the 95% CI runs from about 0.266 to 0.295. The true value is inside the interval. **Part 5** ::: {.cell fit_deps='data'} ```{.r .cell-code} # fit the same ordered logit with brm() fit_brm_ordered <- brm(y ~ income + x2, data = data, family = cumulative("logit"), backend = "cmdstanr", chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 1234) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # posterior means and 95% credible intervals, next to the truth and polr() cbind(truth = c(alpha, b1, b2), polr = c(fit$zeta, coef(fit)), fixef(fit_brm_ordered)[, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` truth polr Estimate Q2.5 Q97.5 1|2 -1.0 -1.000 -1.000 -1.050 -0.952 2|3 0.5 0.511 0.511 0.465 0.557 3|4 2.0 2.018 2.018 1.958 2.080 income 0.4 0.409 0.409 0.387 0.432 x2Label 2 1.0 0.923 0.922 0.843 1.003 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # recover the fd with the brm() fit comparisons(fit_brm_ordered, variables = list(income = c(-1.5, 1.5)), newdata = datagrid(x2 = "Label 1"), hypothesis = "b3 + b4 = 0") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypothesis Estimate 2.5 % 97.5 % b3+b4=0 0.28 0.266 0.295 Type: response ``` ::: ::: The posterior means are very close to the `polr()` estimates. All five true values are inside the 95% credible intervals. The first difference is 0.28 (95% credible interval is [0.266, 0.295]). Truth (0.275) is inside the interval. ::: ## Feelings Toward Donald Trump {ref="trump-feelings"} The dataset [here](https://pos5747.github.io/files/anes-ft-groups.csv) from the 2016 ANES has data on feeling thermometer ratings of Donald Trump and a `social_group` variable that indicates a race-sex-degree triplet. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anes_ft <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/anes-ft-groups.csv") |> glimpse() ``` ::: I'm interested in the feelings of each group toward Donald Trump. You can see that the sample averages and sample sizes vary a lot across the groups.^[Three of the *possible* groups have zero observations.] ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tinytable) anes_ft |> group_by(social_group) |> summarize(`Number of Respondents` = n(), `Sample Average` = mean(ft_donald_trump)) |> rename(`Social Group` = social_group) |> arrange(desc(`Number of Respondents`)) |> tt(digits = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Use a hierarchical model to estimate the average for each group. ::: sol ::: {.cell fit_deps='anes_ft'} ```{.r .cell-code} f <- ft_donald_trump ~ (1 | social_group) fit_trump <- brm(f, data = anes_ft, chains = 4, cores = 4, backend = "cmdstanr", seed = 1234) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # sample size and sample average for each group group_summaries <- anes_ft |> summarize(n = n(), sample_average = mean(ft_donald_trump), .by = social_group) # hierarchical estimate for each group, next to the sample average p_trump <- predictions(fit_trump, newdata = datagrid(social_group = unique)) |> as_tibble() |> select(social_group, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) |> left_join(group_summaries, by = "social_group") |> arrange(n) p_trump ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 15 × 6 social_group estimate conf.low conf.high n sample_average 1 White; Other; College Degree 26.3 -0.659 50.8 2 8 2 Other; Other; No College De… 26.5 2.38 49.1 3 15.7 3 White; Other; No College De… 31.6 9.36 52.4 4 31.2 4 Black; Male; College Degree 20.3 8.48 31.8 28 17.7 5 Black; Female; College Degr… 13.2 5.65 21.4 64 11.6 6 Other; Female; College Degr… 27.1 20.8 33.6 96 26.7 7 Black; Male; No College Deg… 26.8 20.8 33.1 101 26.5 8 Other; Male; College Degree 35.8 30.0 41.7 116 36.0 9 Black; Female; No College D… 21.8 16.6 27.2 142 21.4 10 Other; Female; No College D… 29.5 25.0 33.9 213 29.4 11 Other; Male; No College Deg… 38.3 34.0 42.6 213 38.5 12 White; Male; College Degree 42.3 39.6 45.1 544 42.5 13 White; Female; College Degr… 33.8 31.1 36.3 594 33.8 14 White; Male; No College Deg… 56.4 54.0 58.9 675 56.7 15 White; Female; No College D… 52.3 50.1 54.7 784 52.6 ``` ::: ::: - Small groups are pulled toward the overall average. "White; Other; College Degree" (n = 2) has a sample average of 8 but an estimate of 26. - Large groups barely move. "White; Female; No College Degree" (n = 784): 52.6 and 52.3. ::: ## Red State, Blue State: Part 6 {ref="red-state-part-6"} In [Part 4](wk09-exercises.html#ex-10), we fit a separate logit in each state using CES data. Now, we'll fit one hierarchical model to all 50 states. Each state will have its own intercept, and we'll model the 50 intercepts using a normal distribution. ::: aside This is the varying-intercept model behind Figure 3 of Gelman et al. (2007, p. 355) [[pdf](https://pos5747.github.io/notes/readings/Gelman2007.pdf)]. ::: `rs_state_median_income` is a state-level measure of income that varies only across states. This is state median household income, rescaled to mean 0 and SD 0.5 across the 50 states. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load data; 50 states ces <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/red-state-part4.csv") # make a state-level data set states <- ces |> distinct(state_name, state_abbr, state_median_income) |> mutate(rs_state_median_income = arm::rescale(state_median_income)) |> glimpse() # add rescaled state income to the voters ces <- ces |> left_join(select(states, state_name, rs_state_median_income), by = "state_name") |> glimpse() ``` ::: 1. Use `brm()` to fit the logit `vote_rep ~ rs_state_median_income + (1 | state_name)`. Use `family = bernoulli`, `backend = "cmdstanr"`, `iter = 10000`, and `warmup = 2000`. Check R-hat and the ESS. 1. Use `predictions()` to compute Pr(Trump), with a 90% CI, for a voter in each state. Plot these 50 estimates and their CIs against `state_median_income`, labeled with the state abbreviations. 1. Add a line for a typical state (i.e., a state whose intercept is exactly what state income predicts). Use `predictions()` with `re_formula = NA` over a range of state incomes. 1. Interpret the coefficient for `rs_state_median_income`. What is the vertical distance between a state's point and the line? 1. Gelman et al. (2007) say that richer states lean Democratic. Does this model show this for 2024? ::: sol **Part 1** ::: {.cell fit_deps='ces'} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_ces <- brm(vote_rep ~ rs_state_median_income + (1 | state_name), data = ces, family = bernoulli, backend = "cmdstanr", iter = 10000, warmup = 2000, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 1234) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(fit_ces) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Family: bernoulli Links: mu = logit Formula: vote_rep ~ rs_state_median_income + (1 | state_name) Data: ces (Number of observations: 48582) Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 10000; warmup = 2000; thin = 1; total post-warmup draws = 32000 Multilevel Hyperparameters: ~state_name (Number of levels: 50) Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS sd(Intercept) 0.26 0.03 0.20 0.33 1.00 4869 10000 Regression Coefficients: Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Intercept -0.26 0.04 -0.33 -0.18 1.00 2892 rs_state_median_income -0.44 0.08 -0.60 -0.29 1.00 3742 Tail_ESS Intercept 6547 rs_state_median_income 7277 Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1). ``` ::: ::: R-hat is 1.00; smallest bulk ESS above 2,000. **Part 2** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # pr(trump) with a 90% ci in each state; one row per state p_ces <- predictions(fit_ces, newdata = states, conf_level = 0.9) |> as_tibble() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gg_ces <- ggplot(p_ces, aes(x = state_median_income, y = estimate)) + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0, color = "grey70") + geom_text(aes(label = state_abbr), size = 3) + labs(x = "State median household income ($1,000s)", y = "Pr(Trump)\n(90% CI)") gg_ces ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](wk10-exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: **Part 3** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # state incomes from the poorest state to the richest, rescaled like rs_state_median_income # (by hand: arm::rescale() would use the grid's own mean and sd, not the states') line_grid <- tibble(state_median_income = seq(min(states$state_median_income), max(states$state_median_income), length.out = 50)) |> mutate(rs_state_median_income = (state_median_income - mean(states$state_median_income)) / (2 * sd(states$state_median_income))) # a typical state: every state's deviation set to zero line_ces <- predictions(fit_ces, newdata = line_grid, re_formula = NA, conf_level = 0.9) |> as_tibble() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # add the line for a typical state to the plot from part 2 gg_ces + geom_ribbon(data = line_ces, aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2) + geom_line(data = line_ces) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](wk10-exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: **Part 4** - The slope coefficient for `rs_state_median_income` is −0.44. Richer states have lower Pr(Trump). This is the slope of the line (but on the logit scale; the plot is on the probability scale.) - Distance from the line: the part of the state's intercept that state income doesn't explain (again, on the probability scale, however). These distances are the "varying" part of the varying intercept. **Part 5** - Yes. The coefficient is negative, and its 95% CI (−0.60 to −0.29) excludes zero. ::: ## Red State, Blue State: Part 7 {ref="red-state-part-7"} Fit the same hierarchical model from [red-state-part-6]{.ex-ref} using the much smaller ANES data set. Create the plot showing the state-level estimates as state income varies. Compare the results to the larger CES dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load data; add rescaled state income from part 6 anes <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/red-state-part5.csv") |> left_join(select(states, state_name, rs_state_median_income), by = "state_name") ``` ::: ::: sol ::: {.cell fit_deps='anes'} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_anes <- brm(vote_rep ~ rs_state_median_income + (1 | state_name), data = anes, family = bernoulli, backend = "cmdstanr", iter = 10000, warmup = 2000, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 1234) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(fit_anes) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Family: bernoulli Links: mu = logit Formula: vote_rep ~ rs_state_median_income + (1 | state_name) Data: anes (Number of observations: 2445) Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 10000; warmup = 2000; thin = 1; total post-warmup draws = 32000 Multilevel Hyperparameters: ~state_name (Number of levels: 50) Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS sd(Intercept) 0.23 0.07 0.09 0.37 1.00 11147 12201 Regression Coefficients: Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Intercept -0.18 0.06 -0.29 -0.06 1.00 27276 rs_state_median_income -0.61 0.12 -0.85 -0.37 1.00 28790 Tail_ESS Intercept 23063 rs_state_median_income 23136 Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1). ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # pr(trump) with a 90% ci in each state, and the line; same grids as part 6 p_anes <- predictions(fit_anes, newdata = states, conf_level = 0.9) |> as_tibble() line_anes <- predictions(fit_anes, newdata = line_grid, re_formula = NA, conf_level = 0.9) |> as_tibble() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # stack the two surveys p_both <- bind_rows(list(CES = p_ces, ANES = p_anes), .id = "survey") |> mutate(survey = factor(survey, levels = c("CES", "ANES"))) line_both <- bind_rows(list(CES = line_ces, ANES = line_anes), .id = "survey") |> mutate(survey = factor(survey, levels = c("CES", "ANES"))) ggplot(p_both, aes(x = state_median_income, y = estimate)) + geom_ribbon(data = line_both, aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2) + geom_line(data = line_both) + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0, color = "grey70") + geom_text(aes(label = state_abbr), size = 2.5) + facet_wrap(vars(survey)) + labs(x = "State median household income ($1,000s)", y = "Pr(Trump)\n(90% CI)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](wk10-exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=1056} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the coefficient in each survey, with 90% intervals coefs <- "b_rs_state_median_income" posterior_summary(fit_ces, variable = coefs, probs = c(0.05, 0.95)) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Est.Error Q5 Q95 b_rs_state_median_income -0.44 0.078 -0.569 -0.313 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} posterior_summary(fit_anes, variable = coefs, probs = c(0.05, 0.95)) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Est.Error Q5 Q95 b_rs_state_median_income -0.614 0.122 -0.811 -0.411 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # median width of the 90% cis tibble(survey = c("CES", "ANES"), median_width = c(median(p_ces$conf.high - p_ces$conf.low), median(p_anes$conf.high - p_anes$conf.low))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 survey median_width 1 CES 0.0585 2 ANES 0.150 ``` ::: ::: - The surveys agree on the overall pattern. Richer states, lower Pr(Trump). Slope: −0.61 (ANES) and −0.44 (CES), with overlapping 90% intervals. - ANES CIs are about 2.5 times as wide (median 0.150 vs. 0.059). - ANES points sit close to the line. About 50 respondents per state on average, so each state's intercept is pulled most of the way to what state income predicts. For the CES, which has about 1,000 per state on average, the points are more scattered. :::
